title: Using Knowledge-Building Curriculum Doesn't Guarantee 'Robust' Reading Comprehension
author: Natalie Wexler
source: Minding the Gap on Substack, December 18, 2025
summary: Wexler reports on an SRI study finding that even with strong content-rich curricula in place, about two-thirds of observed reading comprehension lessons were surface-level rather than robust. Surface lessons focus on completing literacy-standards tasks (describe the setting, identify nonliteral language); robust lessons keep meaning in the foreground and recruit whatever skills are needed to understand it. The cause is not the curriculum but implementation; teachers are modifying lessons to put skills-based standards back in the foreground, often at the urging of professional-learning providers and benchmark-test protocols. Forty-seven percent of teachers reported modifying half or more of a comprehension lesson, compared with 13 percent for foundational skills. Wexler's remedies are practical: deepen teachers' own content knowledge by having them read and discuss the texts their students will read, make sure coaches understand the content, use model lessons and video, pay attention to the curriculum's own assessments rather than letting benchmark tests drive instruction. Her closing is pointed: content-rich curriculum is necessary but not sufficient for robust comprehension; the question of what teachers actually do with the text is where quality is decided.
points: Content-rich curriculum is necessary but not sufficient for robust reading comprehension; the quality of comprehension instruction is decided by what teachers actually do with the text.
Teachers are modifying comprehension lessons to put skills-based standards back in the foreground, turning content-rich lessons into surface-level skill practice.
Robust comprehension instruction puts meaning in the foreground and recruits whatever skills help students understand it, rather than teaching skills as the primary goal.
quotes: Robust” comprehension instruction, in contrast, might have students engage in some of those tasks, but the focus is on the overall meaning of the text. In other words, instead of using a text to teach a skill, a lesson that leads to robust comprehension puts the text in the foreground, bringing in whatever skills might help students understand and analyze that text.

According to a companion report from SRI, 47 percent of teachers said they modified half or more of a comprehension lesson, compared to only 13 percent who said they did so with a lesson in foundational reading skills like phonics. That report also found that many teachers viewed the comprehension aspect of their curriculum more difficult to implement, saying the texts were “too dense” and complex for their students.

Kristen McQuillan, a consultant who has worked with districts implementing knowledge-building curricula, says that from her observations, it's clear the curricula themselves aren't the reason so many lessons are surface-level. In many cases, she says, “teachers are changing the curriculum in pursuit of how to help kids master the standards.

One problem is that identifying character traits isn't a skill you can “master.” It will be easier or harder depending on the particular text. Another, McQuillan said, is that kids can get confused if the lesson objective is too “meta.

Like the state assessments, these tests present students with reading passages unrelated to anything they might have learned through the curriculum and provide teachers with data framed entirely in terms of the skills in literacy standards. They might tell teachers that students are weak in a skill like identifying the main idea of a text, when in fact the student might not have understood the text because of a lack of relevant background knowledge.

So while content-rich, knowledge-building curriculum doesn't guarantee robust instruction, it's crucial to enabling that kind of instruction to happen. Professional learning is also vital, for coaches and administrators as well as teachers.” Archived from Minding the Gap on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
